b: I did my first Oklahoma Drill in seventh grade at Sequoyah Middle School in Edmond, OK. It was the first day of pads on what I’m sure was a sweltering August afternoon.
The coach and his assistants set up the drill the way it’s been set up on football practice fields across the country since its inception:

Tackling dummies are laid on the ground about three yards apart, forming a narrow chute. A blocker and a defender line up face to face inside it. A ball carrier stands a few yards behind the blocker holding a football. On the whistle, the blocker tries to drive the defender back while the defender tries to shed him and make the tackle. The runner looks for a crease…or he can just run right into the defender at full speed and knock him on his ass; the drill both simulates the dynamics of real football play, and is just a who’s-got-the-grit jousting contest.

The coach had the rest of the team form a circle around the drill, creating a scene that looked like an after-school fight. For 45 minutes, three 13-year-old boys at a time would take turns stepping into the makeshift arena to see who had the right stuff while their teammates would whoop and holler or give a collective “OOOOOOOHHHHHH!!” when a particularly vicious hit was made.

Up until this point in my life, I’d never blocked or tackled anybody in football pads at full speed before. While I waited for my turn, I had butterflies in my stomach and sweaty palms. I watched my teammates carefully to figure out how to approach the drill when it was my turn so that 1) I didn’t look like an idiot, and 2) I didn’t die.

When it was my turn, I was marked as the defender. Thankfully, the blocker in front of me was a guy a bit smaller and slightly less athletic than me. “I’ll be able to shuck this guy and at least get a tackle on the runner,” I thought.

Unthankfully, the runner was Evan, a Little League teammate of mine who happened to be one of the biggest and fastest kids on the football team. “Cornfed” would be how you’d describe him. He had a beard and visible deltoid muscles, while I had peach fuzz and the soft doughy arms of a kid who wore size “husky” underpants from Sears. In other words, Evan was a man, and I was a mere boy. A pit in my stomach formed.

The whistle blew. I easily shucked my blocker as I predicted and felt a swell of pride at the win. But it was a pyrrhic victory since it put me right in the path of Evan, who was barreling straight at me.
I started to say a silent prayer in my mind: Please let him juke. Please let him juke. Please let him juke.
Evan did not juke. He absolutely railroaded me.
I saw stars just like in the cartoons.
The next thing I remember, I was on my back. Am I dead? Am I paralyzed?

After verifying that I was neither deceased nor immobilized, I quickly got up off the ground. I wanted to show the guys that I could take a hit and think nothing of it. Manly 13-year-old pride was on the line here. I made a self-deprecating joke as I took my place among the ring of spectators who’d gathered round this American form of single combat, while feeling the sting of embarrassment of having my ass soundly handed to me in front of 50 of my fellow male peers.

I did the Oklahoma Drill plenty more times in middle school and high school, usually on the first day of pads. The Oklahoma Drill is largely banned these days, and I’ve been thinking about it lately both as an interesting bit of cultural history and as an encapsulation of the dilemma of modern rites of passage.
The Father of the Oklahoma Drill: Bud Wilkinson

The Oklahoma Drill gets its name from the University of Oklahoma, where head coach Bud Wilkinson came up with it in the late 1940s. I’m an OU grad and live in Oklahoma, so I’ve always felt a weird sense of pride in the drill.

When Wilkinson took over as head coach for OU in 1947, he introduced a 5-2 defense. Most teams back then lined up six down linemen who each covered one gap. Wilkinson wanted his linebackers free to read the play, so his interior linemen had to control two gaps at once, which meant beating a blocker in tight quarters and still making the tackle.

He also wanted a drill to find out who had the dog in them. In the Navy, Wilkinson had served in the V-5 pre-flight program, which used boxing and wrestling to weed out cadets who lacked aggression. Wilkinson used the Oklahoma Drill the same way. It was a sorting tool to see which players had the right stuff.

And the drill seemed to work. From 1953 to 1957, the Sooners won 47 games in a row, which is still the college football record. Before long, the Oklahoma Drill was being used by other colleges and started filtering up to the NFL and filtering down to high school and peewee teams.
Coaches loved the Oklahoma Drill. First, they thought it instilled good, hard-nosed defensive technique. But mostly coaches liked it because they thought of it as a man-maker.
Vince Lombardi saw the drill as a measure of manhood.
Bill Belichick summed up the appeal of the Oklahoma Drill with three questions: “Who is a man? Who’s tough? Who’s going to hit somebody?”

Barry Switzer, another legendary OU football coach, said that the Oklahoma Drill was “one of the few Neanderthal drills that I still believe in. You learn all you need to know about a player and you learn it in a hurry.”

So the Oklahoma Drill was both athletic practice and rite of passage. When masculine reputation, honor, is on the line, men (and boys) will do whatever it takes to win. And the way to do that is to put your hat on the other guy’s hat as hard as you can.
Unfortunately, that’s also a good way to get injured.
The Fall of the Oklahoma Drill

The constraints of the Oklahoma Drill force high-speed collisions. And those repeated collisions cause damage. Over the years, there have been some high-profile cases of athletes getting severely injured or even dying from participating in the Oklahoma Drill.

Such cases prompted a push to get rid of it. On top of that, growing research in the past few decades has shown the connection between repeated blows to the head and chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a degenerative brain disease. Research suggests it’s not just concussions that matter, but the cumulative impact of thousands of hits over a career, including hits that don’t cause concussions. Practice exercises like the Oklahoma Drill produce lots of repeated hard hits, particularly helmet-to-helmet ones, the kind associated with CTE risk.

The NFL banned the drill in 2019. The NCAA followed in 2021. Both leagues concluded that the straight-line collisions typical of the Oklahoma Drill rarely happen in games, so practicing for those kinds of hits was pretty pointless. USA Football now tells youth and high school teams to drop it too.
The Oklahoma Drill (And the State of Male Rites of Passage) Today
Many football coaches have swapped out the Oklahoma Drill for rugby-style tackling drills that teach players to hit with the shoulder and keep their heads out of the way.

But the Oklahoma Drill still lives on. At least on social media. If you scroll Instagram or YouTube, you’ll likely come across videos of young guys on a beach running the drill with no pads. Even the chicks get in on the action. You hear the same “OOOOOHHHHHH!” that I did whenever there’s a sick tackle. There’s even an amateur competition similar to those slap competitions where people do the Oklahoma Drill, complete with weight classes and rankings.

Getting rid of the widespread practice of the Oklahoma Drill was probably the right call. But that probably reveals my ambivalence. There’s a part of me that still thinks appreciatively of the Oklahoma Drill, even though I hated it at the time. It viscerally taught me courage and that taking a hit (either physically or psychologically) often isn’t as bad as you’d think it would be. Young men need to learn those kinds of lessons. And try as we might, they’re hard to teach in a “safe” way.

Across time and cultures, rites of passage were developed to inculcate certain attributes in young men, like bravery, resilience, and endurance of pain. A lot of them seem pointlessly dangerous and painful, but they answer a young man’s desire to test and prove himself. We’ve come to a point in society where we’d like for young men to have challenges that don’t involve risk or pain and still feel significant. But it’s impossible to have both. As the risk of an activity goes down, so does its feeling of significance. You could, for example, make the BUD/S training that Navy SEALs undergo so safe and undemanding that no one ever died from it, but then it wouldn’t be as transformative an experience.

How to balance the risk-reward ratio of rites of passage so there isn’t so much risk that the experience seems needlessly reckless, but there is enough risk that it still means something and changes a young man, is a hard nut to crack. We’ve gotten rid of stuff like the Oklahoma Drill, but we haven’t figured out how to replace it.
